text: Guys, first of all, thanks a lot for the activity under my previous video, where I reacted to the viral claim that being pregnant is more dangerous than being a cop. And I'm making this follow-up because there was one elephant in the room that I overlooked and that some of you pointed out in the comments. Quick recap to refresh the memory. The woman in the video compared the police line of duty death rate, around 12.5 per 100,000 officers, with the US maternal mortality rate, which was 18.6 per 100,000 live birth in 2023. So on a surface, pregnancy looked more dangerous. But the elephant in the room you guys pointed out is exposure time. A police officer is usually exposed to job-related risk every year for many years. Pregnancy is usually a temporary exposure. Many women experience it once, twice, or a few times. Not every year for 20 or 30 years. And honestly, I am proud of you guys for pointing this out. Because this is exactly what I'm preaching. Use your critical thinking. Question everyone. Me included. I make mistakes too. Sometimes I miss a strong argument. Sometimes I focus on one part of the issue and overlook another. So yes, this is probably the strongest critique of the comparison. Because if you compare one pregnancy or one birth-related risk to one year of being a police officer, then yes, you can make that comparison in a limited way. But if you make the broader claim that being pregnant is more dangerous than being a cop, then you have to account for exposure time. So if police line of duty mortality is around 12.5 per 100,000 officers per year, then over a 20-year career, a rough cumulative exposure would be around 250 per 100,000 officers. And if maternal mortality is 18.6 per 100,000 live births, and the average US woman has around 1.6 live births, then the rough lifetime exposure would be around 30 per 100,000 women. Suddenly, using these measurements, we can see that being a cop is more than 8 times more dangerous than being pregnant. Now, is this a perfect calculation? No. Of course not. Risks change by age, location, health, race, job assignment, department, year, and many other factors. But as a rough illustration, it shows why the time frame matters. And this is exactly why the viral claim is too clean for something that is actually very messy. Some of you also mentioned other critiques, and I checked those too. For example, yes, it is true that not every police officer has the same level of risk. Some officers patrol dangerous areas, other work safer jobs, administration, IT, office management, and so on. So comparing all cops to all pregnant women can be misleading. But the same logic also applies to pregnancy. Not every pregnancy has the same risk either. Medical complications vary by age, health, prior conditions, access to healthcare, race, and other factors. So that critique is valid, but it cuts both ways. Another point was about police officers analyzing themselves. And yes, it is a real and serious issue, and it is generally not included in line of duty death statistics. But if we start adding broader death connected to the job on the police side, then we also have to be consistent on the pregnancy side. So again, valid point, but we have to apply the same rules to both sides. Overall, you guys brought up some good critiques and additions to the first video. But to me, nothing stood out as much as the exposure time argument. That is the game-changing one. And yes, I know, I still haven't responded to the second part of her fact check, where she talks about whether being the pregnant partner of a police officer is more dangerous than being a cop. I decided to postpone that part, that should be in the next video, because the elephant in the room was too important to just pass by.
